title: Languages, logic and proof
subtitle: The vocabulary everything else is built on: strings, languages, and how to be sure a claim is true.

sections.title: Alphabets, strings and languages
sections.body:
Before we ask what a computer can do, we must agree on what we are asking it to look at. Think of Scrabble: you have a finite bag of letters, and you build words. That is exactly where theory begins.

An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols, e.g. {0, 1}. A string is a finite sequence of them; ε is the empty string (the word with no letters) and Σ* is the set of all strings. A language is any subset of Σ*, for example “all binary strings ending in 01”. Notice that “language” here has nothing to do with English; it is just a chosen collection of strings.

The whole subject asks one question: how complicated a machine is needed to recognise a given language? Warm up: over Σ = {0, 1} how many strings have length exactly 3? Two choices for each of three positions gives 2³ = 8. And the length of the empty string ε is 0.

worked.why: Over Σ = {0, 1} how many strings have length exactly 3?
Two choices for each of three positions.

questions.prompt: What is the length of the empty string ε?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It has no symbol at all.

keynotes: An alphabet Σ is a finite set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence of them, ε is the empty string and Σ* is the set of all strings.
A language is any subset of Σ*, such as all binary strings ending in 01.
The core question is how complicated a machine is needed to recognise a given language; there are 2³ = 8 binary strings of length 3.

sections.title: Operations on languages
sections.body:
Languages are sets, so you can combine them, a bit like mixing paint colours. Given languages L and M, there are three builders. Union L ∪ M takes strings from either. Concatenation LM takes a string of L followed by one of M. And the Kleene star L* joins zero or more strings of L together.

The star deserves a moment. If L = {a, b} then L* contains ε, a, b, aa, ab, … in short, every string over {a, b}. Does L* always contain ε? Yes, because “zero strings joined” is allowed. Keep that in mind; it is a favourite exam trap.

choices.text: Yes — zero repetitions give the empty string.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Even if L itself does not contain ε.

sections.title: Propositional logic and inference
sections.body:
To be sure of anything in this course, you need a trustworthy way to reason. Statements combine with ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (or), → (implies) and ↔ (iff). Then a few rules do all the heavy lifting. Modus ponens: from P and P → Q, conclude Q. Modus tollens: from ¬Q and P → Q, conclude ¬P. De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q. And predicate logic adds ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).

Try one. “If it rains the match is cancelled” (R → C), and “the match was not cancelled” (¬C). Modus tollens gives ¬R: it didn’t rain. Now the trap: from P → Q and Q, what can you conclude about P? Nothing! The match may have been cancelled for another reason.

worked.why: Premises: “if it rains the match is cancelled” (R → C) and “the match was not cancelled” (¬C).

questions.prompt: From P → Q and Q, what can you conclude about P?

choices.text: Nothing — that is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

keynotes: Modus ponens: from P and P → Q conclude Q; modus tollens: from ¬Q and P → Q conclude ¬P; De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q.
Predicate logic adds ∀ (for all) and ∃ (there exists).

sections.title: Proof techniques
sections.body:
How can you be certain that something is true for every case, including the infinitely many you will never test? You need a proof, and there are five tools worth keeping in your pocket.

Direct proof: just argue forward. Contradiction: assume the opposite and derive an absurdity (the classic is that √2 is irrational). Induction: prove a base case and that n ⇒ n+1, like a line of dominoes. The pigeonhole principle: put n+1 pigeons in n holes and some hole has two, the engine behind the pumping lemma. And diagonalisation: build an object that differs from the i-th item in the i-th place, which proves the reals are uncountable and the halting problem undecidable.

Watch induction work on 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. Base n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Step: assume it for n; adding n+1 gives n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2, the formula for n+1. And among 13 people, at least two share a birth month, because of the pigeonhole principle.

worked.why: Base n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2 ✓. Step: assume it for n; adding n+1 gives n(n+1)/2 + (n+1) = (n+1)(n+2)/2, the formula for n+1.

keynotes: Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite and derives an absurdity, e.g. that √2 is irrational.
Induction proves a base case and that n ⇒ n+1: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2.
The pigeonhole principle (n+1 pigeons in n holes) is the engine behind the pumping lemma.
Diagonalisation builds an object that differs from the i-th item in the i-th place, proving the reals uncountable and the halting problem undecidable.

sections.title: The road ahead: the Chomsky hierarchy
sections.body:
Here is the map of the whole course, so you always know where you stand. There are four classes of language, each needing a stronger machine than the one before: regular (finite automaton) ⊂ context-free (pushdown automaton) ⊂ context-sensitive (linear-bounded automaton) ⊂ recursively enumerable (Turing machine).

Each class needs strictly more memory than the one inside it, as the figure shows: nested rings, with the regular languages at the centre. The rest of the course climbs this ladder one rung at a time. Which machine recognises exactly the context-free languages? The pushdown automaton, which you will meet in chapter 3.

questions.prompt: Which machine recognises exactly the context-free languages?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A finite control plus one stack.

figures.caption: Figure 1.5.1 — the Chomsky hierarchy
figures.note: Each class needs strictly more memory than the one inside it.

keynotes: Four classes of language, each needing a stronger machine: regular (finite automaton), context-free (pushdown automaton), context-sensitive (linear-bounded automaton) and recursively enumerable (Turing machine).
Each class needs strictly more memory than the one inside it.
The pushdown automaton recognises exactly the context-free languages.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Before we climb, check your pack.

  • A language is a set of strings over an alphabet; ∪, concatenation and * build new ones.
  • Proofs: direct, contradiction, induction, pigeonhole, diagonalisation.

If you can say in your own words what each of the five proof styles is for, you are ready.
keynotes: A language is a set of strings over an alphabet, and union, concatenation and star build new ones.
Proofs: direct, contradiction, induction, pigeonhole and diagonalisation.
